qt: to the Commission Ton Diepeveen (PfE) Subject:

Under the Commission’s proposal, only natural persons may be appointed as directors of an EU Inc. In several Member States, however, it is possible for legal persons to act as directors of a company. By excluding this possibility for the EU Inc., legal persons who, under national law, are directors of a company incorporated under national law are excluded from holding a comparable directorship in an EU Inc. This raises questions about the compatibility of this restriction with the aim of establishing the EU Inc. as an attractive and legally neutral alternative to national company forms. 1.
Why has the Commission chosen to categorically exclude legal persons from acting as directors of an EU Inc., even though this is permitted in several Member States?
How does the Commission assess the risk that this restriction will lead to unequal treatment of companies or legal persons which, under national law, are permitted to act as directors?

Is the Commission prepared to amend the proposed rules so that legal persons may also be appointed as directors of an EU Inc., provided that appropriate rules on representation, responsibility and liability are put in place?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2026) The objective of the EU Inc. proposal is to establish one single set of rules for an EU legal form, which entails the harmonization of rules across all 27 Member States. The proposal provides for an optional legal form which co-exist with other national legal forms. The founders may choose which legal form best suits their needs. The proposal provides that only natural persons may be appointed as directors of an EU Inc. and thus harmonises this aspect for EU Inc. companies. As to the Member States’ rules, currently the majority of Member States’ laws require directors to be only natural persons. By requiring directors to be natural persons, the proposal ensures that rules such as those related to disclosure, disqualification and representation can be effectively applied. It also ensures a direct human accountability and an effective enforcement of personal liability of directors. As to the groups of companies, while legal persons as directors are used in some Member States as a group management mechanism, this issue is addressed in the EU Inc. proposal through the possibility of the General Meeting to issue binding instruction to the directors. Allowing a director to be a legal person introduces practical enforcement issues, requires introduction of rules on the person who acts on the behalf of the legal person and potentially facilitates situations leading to abuse or fraud. In particular, restricting directorships to natural persons prevents the use of opaque shell or front companies as directors, safeguarding corporate transparency and strengthening anti-money laundering measures. The proposal is now in inter-institutional negotiations.
